transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: My guest today is the novelist James Okoro, whose fourth novel, The Salt Road, has just been published. James, you've said that you don't plan your novels in advance. Is that really true?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Mostly. I start with a situation, usually an image, and I follow it to see what happens. With The Salt Road, it was a woman standing at a railway station waiting for someone who doesn't arrive. I didn't know who she was or why, and that uncertainty is what kept me writing.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Doesn't that lead to a lot of rewriting?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Enormous amounts. The first draft is about twice as long as the final book, and I throw away much of it. But I don't regard that as wasted. The material I cut is how I discover what the book is about. I don't believe writers always know their subject at the start, whatever they claim in interviews.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: You've often been described as a political novelist. Do you accept that label?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Reluctantly. My books are set against political upheaval, and the characters are affected by it, but I'm not trying to argue a position. If I wanted to do that, I'd write essays. A novel, for me, is a way of exploring how people live with things they can't control. If readers come away with a political message, that's their reading, and I don't object, but it isn't my starting point.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: The Salt Road is set in a fictional country. Why invent one?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Two reasons. The practical one is that I'm freed from the obligation to get every historical detail right, which can paralyse a writer. The deeper reason is that a real place brings assumptions with it. Readers think they already know what's going on in a country they've read about in the news. A fictional setting forces them to pay attention to the people instead.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Some critics have praised the novel's restraint. The most painful events happen off the page.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: That was deliberate. I've never found violence on the page convincing; it tends to become either spectacle or sentimentality. What's more interesting is the aftermath, how a family tries to carry on at breakfast the next morning. I trust readers to feel the enormity of what's happened without being told.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: I used to, obsessively. Now I read a handful from people whose judgement I trust, and ignore the rest. Praise is pleasant but doesn't teach you much, whereas a thoughtful criticism can change how I write the next book.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: What advice would you give to aspiring writers?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Read widely, including things you don't expect to enjoy. And finish things. Many people start novels, but few reach the end of a draft, and it's only then you learn how to revise. A bad finished draft is worth more than a brilliant unfinished one.
